source_text: Ecce idem Moyses refert alio in loco, quod Abrahae uisus sit deus. quod nemo hominum deum uideat et utuat. potest deus, quomodo uisus est deus? quomodo uideri non potest? inquit, wdit umguam; hominum nemo, nec uidere potest. mentitur; ergo uere uisus est deus. ex quo intellegi potest, quod non pater uisus sit, qui numquam uisus est, sed filius, qui et descendere solitus est, et uideri quia descenderit. imago ro est enim éinuisibilis dei, ut mediocritas et fragilitas condicionis humanae deum patrem uidere aliquando iam tunc assuesceret in imagine dei, hoc est, in filio dei. gradatim enim et per incrementa fragilitas humana nutriri debuit per imaginem ad istam gloriam, ut deum patrem uidere possit aliquando, periculosa sunt enim quae magna sunt, si repentina sunt. nam etiam lux solis subita post tenebras splendore nimio insuetis oculis non ostendet diem, sed potius faciet caecitatem. quod ne in damnum humanorum contingat oculorum, paulatim disruptis et dissipatis tenebris, ortus luminaris istius mediocribus incrementis fallenter assurgens oculos hominum sensim assuefacit ad totum orbem suum ferendum per incrementa radiorum. sic ergo et Christus, id est imago dei et filius dei, ab hominibus inspicitur, qua poterat uideri. et ideo fragilitas et mediocritas sortis humanae per ipsum alitur, producitur, educatur, ut aliquando deum quoque ipsum patrem, assueta filium conspicere, possit, w est, uidere; ne maiestatis ipsius repentino et intolerabili fulgore percussa intercipi possit, ut deum patrem quem semper optauit uidere non possit. ex quo filius est hic qui uidetur; dei autem filius, dei uerbum est; dei autem uerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. quae, malum, ratio est ut dubitetur deus dici, qui tot modis deus intellegitur approbari? Ac si et Agar ancillam Sarae de domo eiectam pariter et fugatam angelus conuenit apud fontem aquae in uia Sur, fugae causas interrogat atque accipit, et post haec humilitatis consilia porrigit, spem praeterea illi materni nominis facit, quodque ex utero eius multum semen esset futurum spondet atque promittit, et quod Hismael ex illa nasci haberet, et cum ceteris aperit locum habitationis ipsius, actumque describit: hunc autem angelum et dominum scriptura proponit et deum (nam nec benedictionem seminis promisisset, nisi angelus et deus fuisset): quaerant quid in praesenti loco haeretici tractent. - pater fuit iste qui ab Agar uisus est, an non? quia deus positus sed absit deum patrem angelum dicere; ne alteri subsed angelum dicent fuisse. quomodo ergo deus erit, si angelus fuit, cum non sit hoc nomen angelis umquam concessum? nisi quoniam ex utroque latere nos ueritas in istam concludit sententiam, qua intellegere debeamus dei filium fuisse: qui, quoniam ex deo est, merito deus, quia dei filius, dictus sit, quoniam patri subditus et annuntiator paternae uoluntatis est, magni consilii angelus pronuntiatus est. ergo si hic locus neque personae patris congruit, ne angelus dictus sit, neque personae angeli, ne, deus pronuntiatus sit; personae autem Christi conuenit ut et deus sit, quia dei filius est, et angelus sit, quoniam paternae dispositionis annuntiator est: intellegere debent contra scripturas se agere haeretici, qui Christum cum dicant se et angelum credere, nolint illum etiam deum pronuntiare, quem in ueteri testamento ad uisitationem generis humani legunt\ saepe uenisse. Adhuc adiecit Moyses, Abrahae uisum deum apud quercum Mambre, sedente ipso ad ostium tabernaculi sui meridie, et nihilominus, cum tres conspexisset uiros, unum ex illis dominum nuncupasse; quorum cum pedes lauisset, cinericios panes cum butyro et ipsius copia lactis offert, et ut hospites retenti uescerentur, hortatur. post quae et quod pater futurus esset, audit; et quod Sara uxor eius paritura ex ipso filium esset, ediscit; et de exitu Sodomitarum, quae merebantur pati, recognoscit; et quod propter clamorem Sodomorum deus descendisset, addiscit. quo in loco si patrem uolunt uideri tunc fuisse cum angelis duobus hospitio receptum, patrem uisibilem haeretici crediderunt: si autem angelum, cum ex angelis tribus unus dominus nuncupatur, cur, quod non solet, angelus deus dicitur? nisi quoniam, ut deo patri inuisibilitas propria reddatur, et angelo propria mediocritas remittatur, non nisi dei filius, qui et deus est, Abrahae uisus et hospitio receptus esse credetur. quod enim erat futurus, meditabatur in sacramento Abrahae factus hospes, apud Abrahae filios futurus; cuius filiorum pedes, ad probationem quod ipse esset, abluit; reddens in filiis ius hospitalitatis, quod aliquando illi fenerauerat pater. unde et ne qua esset dubitatio quin iste Abrahae hospes fuisset, in Sodomitarum exitu ponitur: quoniam pluit dominus super Sodomam et Gomorram ignem et sulphur a domino de caelo. sic enim et prophetes ex persona dei: subuerti uos, inquit, sécut subuertit dominus Sodomam et Gomorram. dominus ergo Sodomam subuertit, id est, deus Sodomam subuertit: sed.in subuersione Sodomorum dominus pluit ignem a domino. hic autem dominus uisus est Abrahae deus: deus autem hic hospes est Abrahae uisus utique quia tactus. sed cum pater, quia inuisibilis, nec tunc utique uisus sit, uisus est et hospitio receptus et acceptus est, qui solitus est tangi et uideri: hic autem filius dei dominus a domino pluit super Sodomam et Gomorram sulphur atque ignem. hic autem dei uerbum est: uerbum autem dei caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. non pater igitur apud Abraham hospes, sed Christus fuit; nec tunc pater uisus est, sed filius; uisus autem est Christus. merito igitur Christus et dominus et deus est, qui non aliter Abrahae uisus est, nisi quia ante ipsum Abraham ex patre deo deus sermo generatus est. Adhuc, inquit, idem angelus et deus eandem Agar, fugatam de domo Abrahae cum puero, consolatur et uisitat. nam cum illa in solitudine exposuisset infantem, quia aqua defecisset ex utre, cumque puer ille clamasset, fletum et planctum leuasset, et audiuit, inquit scriptura, deus uocem pueri ae loco ubi erat. cum deum esse, qui uocem audisset infantis, rettulisset, adiecit: et uocauit angelus domini ipsam Agar de caelo; angelum referens esse quem deum dixerat, et~dominum pronuntians esse quem angelum collocarat.. quique angelus et deus adhuc ipsi Agar promittit maiora solacia, dicendo: ne timueris; exaudiui enim uocem pueri de loco ubi erat. surge, sume puerum, et tene: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum. hic angelus, si angelus tantum est, cur hoc sibi uindicat ut dicat: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum, cum hoc utique genus potentiae dei sit, angeli esse non possit? ex quo etiam deus confirmatur esse qui hoc potest facere. quoniam ut hoc ipsum comprobetur, adicitur per scripturam statim: e aperuit deus oculos eius, et uidit puteum aquae uiuae, et abiit, et impleuit utrem de puteo, et dedit puero, et erat deus cum puero. si ergo hic deus erat cum puero, qui aperuit oculos Agar, ut uideret puteum aquae uiuae et hauriret aquam propter urgentem sitis necessitatem; hic autem deus e caelo illam uocat; angelus dictus, cum superius uocem audiens clamantis pueri deus esset potius, non alius intellegitur quam angelus esse pariter et deus. quod cum patri competens et conueniens esse non possit, qui tantummodo deus est, competens autem esse possit Christo, qui non tantummodo deus sed et angelus pronuntiatus est, manifeste apparet non patrem ibi tunc locutum fuisse ad Agar, sed Christum potius, cum deus sit, cui etiam angeli competit nomen, quippe cum magni consili angelus factus sit; angelus autem sit, dum exponit sinum patris, sicut Ioannes edicit. si enim ipse Ioannes hunc eundem, qui sinum exponit patris, uerbum dicit carnem factum esse, ut sinum patris posset exponere, merito Christus non solum homo est, sed et angelus; nec angelus tantum, sed et deus per scripturas ostenditur, et a nobis hoc esse creditur, ne, si non Christum tunc locutum ad Agar uoluerimus accipere, aut angelum deum faciamus, aut deum patrem omnipotentem inter angelos computemus.
pass_a_gloss: Behold, Moses also reports in another place that God was seen by Abraham. That no man can see God and live. How can God be seen, since God cannot be seen? He says that no man has ever seen Him; no one can see Him. He is lying; therefore, God was truly seen. From this, it can be understood that it was not the Father who was seen, who has never been seen, but the Son, who is accustomed to descend and be seen because He descended. For the image of the invisible God is so that the mediocrity and fragility of the human condition might gradually become accustomed to seeing God the Father in the image of God, that is, in the Son of God. For human fragility had to be nourished gradually through the image to this glory, so that it might be able to see God the Father someday, because great things are dangerous if they are sudden. For even the light of the sun, after darkness, does not show the day to unaccustomed eyes with too much splendor, but rather causes blindness. So that this might not happen to the detriment of human eyes, with the darkness gradually broken and dispersed, the rising of this light, with moderate increments, gently rising, gradually accustoms human eyes to bear its entire orb through the increments of its rays. Thus, Christ, who is the image of God and the Son of God, is seen by men insofar as He can be seen. And therefore, the fragility and mediocrity of the human condition are nourished, produced, and educated through Him, so that someday, having become accustomed to seeing the Son, it might be able to see God the Father Himself; lest it be struck by the sudden and intolerable splendor of His majesty and be unable to see God the Father, whom it has always desired to see. From this, it is the Son who is seen; but the Son of God is the Word of God; and the Word of God was made flesh and dwelled among us: this is Christ. What evil reasoning is it to doubt that He is called God, who is approved as God in so many ways? And if the angel met Hagar, the servant of Sarah, who was cast out and fled from her home, at the spring of water on the road to Sur, and asked her the reasons for her flight, and received them, and after these things, offered her counsel of humility, and gave her hope of the name of mother, and promised that there would be a great multitude of offspring from her, and that Ishmael would be born from her, and showed her the place of her habitation, and described her actions: let the heretics examine what is being treated in this present passage. Was it the Father who was seen by Hagar, or not? Because God is mentioned, but it is absurd to say that God the Father is an angel; lest they say that another angel was present. How, then, can He be God if He was an angel, since this name has never been given to angels? Unless, indeed, the truth from both sides concludes us to this sentence, that we ought to understand it was the Son of God: who, because He is from God, is rightly called God, because He is the Son of God; and because He is subject to the Father and the announcer of the Father's will, He is proclaimed to be the angel of great counsel. Therefore, if this passage does not fit the person of the Father, lest He be called an angel, nor the person of an angel, lest He be called God; but it fits the person of Christ, that He is God, because He is the Son of God, and an angel, because He is the announcer of the Father's disposition: the heretics ought to understand that they are acting against the Scriptures, who say they believe Christ is an angel, but do not want to proclaim Him God, whom they read in the Old Testament to have come often to visit the human race. Moreover, Moses added that God was seen by Abraham at the oak of Mamre, while he was sitting at the door of his tent at noon, and nonetheless, when he saw three men, he called one of them Lord; and when he washed their feet, he offered them ashes and bread with butter, and an abundance of milk, and encouraged them to eat as guests. After these things, he heard that he would be a father; and that Sarah, his wife, would bear a son from him; and he recognized the outcome of the Sodomites, who deserved to suffer; and he learned that God had descended because of the cry of the Sodomites. In this passage, if they want the Father to have been seen then with the two angels who were received as guests, the heretics have believed in a visible Father: but if it was an angel, since one of the three angels is called Lord, why is the angel called God, which is not usual? Unless, indeed, in order that the invisibility proper to God the Father might be preserved, and the mediocrity proper to the angel might be remitted, it is believed that the Son of God, who is also God, was seen and received as a guest by Abraham. For what was going to happen, He meditated in the sacrament, having become a guest of Abraham, and was going to be among the sons of Abraham; whose feet, as a proof that He Himself was, He washed; rendering the right of hospitality in the sons, which the Father had once provided. Whence, also, so that there might be no doubt that this guest of Abraham was He, it is stated in the outcome of the Sodomites: that the Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord in heaven. Thus, the prophet speaks in the person of God: 'I will overthrow you,' he says, 'as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.' Therefore, the Lord overthrew Sodom, that is, God overthrew Sodom: but in the overthrow of the Sodomites, the Lord rained fire from the Lord. But this Lord was seen by Abraham as God; and God is the guest who was seen by Abraham, certainly because He was touched. But since the Father, because He is invisible, was not seen then, He who is accustomed to be touched and seen was seen and received as a guest: this Lord, however, is the Son of God, who rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord. But this is the Word of God: and the Word of God was made flesh and dwelled among us: this is Christ. Therefore, it was not the Father who was the guest with Abraham, but Christ; and it was not the Father who was seen then, but the Son; and Christ was seen. Therefore, Christ is rightly Lord and God, who was seen by Abraham in no other way than because, before Abraham, the Word of God was generated from God the Father. Moreover, it is said that the same angel and God consoled and visited Hagar, who was cast out from Abraham's home with her child. For when she had exposed the infant in the wilderness, because the water had failed from her skin, and the child had cried out, and she had raised her lamentation, and the Scripture says that God heard the voice of the child from the place where he was. When it had been said that it was God who heard the voice of the infant, it was added: and the angel of the Lord called her, Hagar, from heaven; referring to the angel as the one whom He had called God, and proclaiming Him to be the Lord whom He had placed as an angel. And this angel and God promised Hagar greater solace, saying: 'Do not fear; for I have heard the voice of the child from the place where he was. Rise, take the child, and hold him; for I will make him a great nation.' If this angel is only an angel, why does He claim for Himself the power to say: 'I will make him a great nation,' since this is a kind of power that belongs to God, and cannot belong to an angel? From which it is also confirmed that He is God, who can do this. For in order that this very thing might be proven, it is added through the Scripture immediately: 'And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water, and she went and filled her skin from the well, and gave it to the child, and God was with the child.' If, then, this was God who was with the child, who opened Hagar's eyes so that she might see the well of living water and draw water because of the urgent necessity of thirst; and this God called her from heaven; and the angel is called, since, above, God was hearing the voice of the crying child, it is not understood to be another than the angel who is also God. Which, since it is fitting and suitable for the Father, who is only God, cannot be; but it can be suitable for Christ, who is not only God but also proclaimed to be an angel, it clearly appears that it was not the Father who spoke then to Hagar, but rather Christ, since He is God, to whom the name of angel is also suitable, since He has been made the angel of great counsel; and He is an angel, since He reveals the bosom of the Father, as John declares. For if John himself says that this same one, who reveals the bosom of the Father, is the Word made flesh, so that He might reveal the bosom of the Father, it is right that Christ is not only man but also angel; and not only angel, but also God, as is shown through the Scriptures, and is believed by us, lest, if we do not want to accept that Christ spoke then to Hagar, we either make an angel God, or count God the Father, who is omnipotent, among the angels.

pass_b_english: Behold, Moses also reports in another place that God was seen by Abraham. Yet no man can see God and live. How, then, can God be seen, if God cannot be seen? Scripture says that no one has ever seen Him, and no one can see Him. If that is an absolute rule, then the account is lying; therefore, God was truly seen. From this we can understand that it was not the Father who was seen, for the Father has never been seen, but the Son, who is accustomed to descend and to be seen because He has descended. For He is the image of the invisible God, so that the mediocrity and fragility of the human condition might gradually become accustomed to seeing God the Father in the image of God — that is, in the Son of God (John 1:14; Colossians 1:15). Human fragility had to be nourished gradually through that image toward this glory, so that it might someday be able to see God the Father, because great things are dangerous if they are sudden. Even the light of the sun, after darkness, does not show the day to unaccustomed eyes with its excessive splendor, but rather causes blindness. Lest this happen to the detriment of human eyes, the rising of this light, with the darkness gradually broken and dispersed, ascending by moderate increments, gently accustoms human eyes to bear its entire orb through the increments of its rays. Thus Christ, who is the image of God and the Son of God, is seen by men insofar as He can be seen. And therefore the fragility and mediocrity of the human condition are nourished, produced, and educated through Him, so that someday, having become accustomed to seeing the Son, it might also be able to see God the Father Himself; lest it be struck by the sudden and intolerable splendor of His majesty and be prevented from seeing God the Father, whom it has always desired to see. From this it follows that the Son is the one who is seen; but the Son of God is the Word of God; and the Word of God was made flesh and dwelt among us: this is Christ (John 1:14). What evil reasoning is it to doubt that He is called God, who is approved as God in so many ways?

Consider also Hagar, the servant of Sarah, cast out and fleeing from her home. An angel met her at the spring of water on the road to Shur, questioned her about the reasons for her flight, received her answer, offered her counsel of humility, gave her hope of the name of mother, promised that her offspring would be exceedingly numerous, that Ishmael would be born to her, and showed her the place of her habitation, describing her future (Genesis 16:7–14). Let the heretics examine what is at stake in this passage. Was it the Father who was seen by Hagar, or not? God is named there, but it is absurd to say that God the Father is an angel; lest they claim another angel was present. How, then, can He be God if He was an angel, since the name 'God' has never been granted to angels? Unless, indeed, the truth from both sides compels us to this conclusion: that we must understand it was the Son of God. Because He is from God, He is rightly called God, since He is the Son of God; and because He is subject to the Father and the announcer of the Father's will, He is proclaimed the Angel of Great Counsel (Isaiah 9:6). Therefore, if this passage fits neither the person of the Father — lest He be called an angel — nor the person of an angel — lest He be called God — but fits the person of Christ, who is God because He is the Son of God, and Angel because He is the announcer of the Father's disposition, then the heretics ought to understand that they are acting against the Scriptures. They say they believe Christ is an angel, yet they refuse to proclaim Him God, whom they read in the Old Testament to have come often to visit the human race.

Moreover, Moses adds that God was seen by Abraham at the oak of Mamre, while he was sitting at the door of his tent at noon. When he saw three men, he called one of them Lord; he washed their feet, offered them cakes baked in ashes with butter and an abundance of milk, and urged them to eat as guests (Genesis 18:1). Afterward he heard that he would become a father, and that Sarah his wife would bear a son from him; he learned the fate of the Sodomites, who deserved to suffer, and that God had descended because of the outcry against Sodom. In this passage, if the heretics want the Father to have been seen then, accompanied by two angels received as guests, they have believed in a visible Father. But if it was an angel, since one of the three is called Lord, why is an angel called God, which is not customary? Unless, indeed, in order that the invisibility proper to God the Father might be preserved, and the mediocrity proper to an angel might be set aside, it is believed that the Son of God, who is also God, was seen and received as a guest by Abraham. For what was going to happen, He meditated in the sacrament, having become a guest of Abraham, and was going to be among the sons of Abraham; whose feet, as proof that He Himself was the one, He washed; rendering in the sons the right of hospitality which the Father had once advanced to Him. Therefore, so that there might be no doubt that this guest of Abraham was He, it is stated in the destruction of the Sodomites: the Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord in heaven (Genesis 19:24). Thus the prophet speaks in the person of God: 'I will overthrow you,' he says, 'as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.' Therefore the Lord overthrew Sodom — that is, God overthrew Sodom — but in the overthrow of the Sodomites the Lord rained fire from the Lord. This Lord was seen by Abraham as God; and God is the guest who was seen by Abraham, certainly because He was touched. But since the Father, because He is invisible, was certainly not seen then, the One who is accustomed to be touched and seen was seen and received as a guest: this Lord, however, is the Son of God, who rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord. But this is the Word of God; and the Word of God was made flesh and dwelt among us: this is Christ (John 1:14). Therefore it was not the Father who was the guest with Abraham, but Christ; and it was not the Father who was seen then, but the Son; and Christ was seen. Rightly, then, Christ is Lord and God, who was seen by Abraham in no other way than because, before Abraham, the Word of God was generated from God the Father.

Furthermore, the same Angel and God consoled and visited Hagar, cast out from Abraham's house with her child. When she had exposed the infant in the wilderness because the water had failed from her skin, and the child cried out, and she lifted up her weeping, Scripture says that God heard the voice of the child from the place where he was (Genesis 16:16–17). When it had been said that it was God who heard the infant's voice, it was added: 'And the angel of the Lord called Hagar from heaven' — identifying the angel as the one whom He had called God, and proclaiming Him to be the Lord whom He had designated as an angel. And this Angel and God promised Hagar greater comfort, saying: 'Do not fear; for I have heard the voice of the child from the place where he was. Rise, take the child, and hold him; for I will make him a great nation' (Genesis 16:17–18). If this Angel is only an angel, why does He claim for Himself the power to say, 'I will make him a great nation,' since this is a kind of power that belongs to God and cannot belong to an angel? From this it is also confirmed that He is God, who can do this. In order that this very thing might be proven, Scripture immediately adds: 'And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water, and she went and filled her skin from the well, and gave it to the child, and God was with the child' (Genesis 16:19–20). If, then, this was God who was with the child, who opened Hagar's eyes so that she might see the well of living water and draw water because of the urgent necessity of thirst; and this God called her from heaven; and He is called an angel, since above He was God hearing the voice of the crying child — it is understood to be none other than the Angel who is also God. But this cannot be fitting or suitable for the Father, who is only God; it can be suitable for Christ, who is not only God but also proclaimed to be an Angel. It clearly appears that it was not the Father who spoke then to Hagar, but rather Christ, since He is God, to whom the name of Angel is also suitable, because He has been made the Angel of Great Counsel; and He is an Angel, since He reveals the bosom of the Father, as John declares (John 1:18). For if John himself says that this same One, who reveals the bosom of the Father, is the Word made flesh, so that He might reveal the bosom of the Father, it is right that Christ is not only man but also Angel; and not only Angel, but also God, as is shown through the Scriptures, and is believed by us — lest, if we do not accept that Christ spoke then to Hagar, we either make an angel God, or count God the Father Almighty among the angels.
